anchor: Paul Klee, Pedagogical Sketchbook (Bauhausbuch 2, 1925; Praeger 1953) for the macro-order, verified against the 1960 Praeger text: I Proportionate Line and Structure, II Dimension and Balance, III Gravitational Curve, IV Kinetic and Chromatic Energy. Wassily Kandinsky, Point and Line to Plane (1926) for Part I. Josef Albers, Interaction of Color (1963) for the exercise method of every ARGUMENT. Nake, Nees and Molnar (1965-74) for where chance enters the lineage.
title: The Sketchbook in Drag: point, line, plane, balance, fall, swing, colour, and out
thesis: This course walks the way Paul Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook walks. A point goes for a walk and becomes a line; the line closes into a plane; the plane repeats and becomes structure; structure gets depth and must balance; the balanced body falls along a curve; what falls starts to swing, circle, spiral, sound and glow, and the book ends in colour. Kandinsky named the first three steps (point, line, plane) and Albers gave the method: every chapter is a controlled problem with a visible target, solved in one constrained material and compared side by side. You build each body in GDScript, give it parameters so it becomes a family, write down which two members will look most alike before you render them, and then stand on it, carry it or walk through it. The programming ideas arrive in the order the bodies need them: a point needs a variable, a line needs a function, a walk needs a list, a floor needs a loop, a family needs a class, a balance needs physics, a curve needs your own gravity, a swing needs sine. Klee never had randomness, noise, recursion or a headset. Chance enters where it entered his lineage, as disturbance of a grid you have already built (Nake's Hommage a Paul Klee, 1965). Where his book stops, the course follows Ada's spine out of the sketchbook and says so. 'In drag' means taking Klee's grammar seriously enough to re-assign it: his first part maps active, medial and passive onto brain, muscle and bone and onto male and female; the scene tree does the same with parent and child. You will make the passive part drive.

parts.title: Point, line, plane (Kandinsky; Klee I.1-4)
parts.promise: From a point you place to a plane you can stand on. You learn that the engine calls your code, that everything is an object in a tree, and that a line is a record of a walk.

parts.title: Repetition is structure (Klee I.5-13; Nake, Nees, Molnar)
parts.promise: Repeat a body and it becomes a floor; give it parameters and it becomes a family; disturb the structure and chance appears; articulate it and it becomes an organism. The part ends in a collage of found and made bodies that you export and show.

parts.title: Dimension and balance (Klee II)
parts.promise: The eye, the camera and the standing body: perspective as a fact about eye height, balance as a fact about the centre of mass, and legs that let the passive end drive. The engine's gravity does the work.

parts.title: The gravitational curve (Klee III)
parts.promise: You write gravity yourself: a curve from steps, regions with different laws, a player who climbs, an orbit that leaks energy, and a small complete game about staying upright.

parts.title: Kinetic and chromatic energy (Klee IV; Albers)
parts.promise: Top, pendulum, circle, spiral, sound, the arrow and the field of arrows, then colour and the shader: the motions that do not end.

parts.title: Out of the sketchbook: bodies in drag (spine 11-25)
parts.promise: Where Klee has no page: noise as ground, rules in time, recursion, grammars, generated worlds, soft, implicit, boolean and collective bodies, bodies that learn, the crisis of foundations, entropy, and your own hall in the headset.

tracks.title: Three weeks: the sketchbook's first page
tracks.length: 3 weeks (15 days). Week 1 (Part I, two short chapters a day on the runnable kits): ch01-ch07, plus a scanning / Tilt Brush session whose results wait for ch13. Week 2: ch08, ch09, ch11, ch12, ch13 (export on Thursday). Week 3: mini project, with two critique sessions in the SFPC Code Societies format (Klee's active/passive passage and the blob aesthetic, walked as encounters in Noise_Space_10 and ISO_Metaballs, no code).
tracks.supplied: Named, not taught: the walker and XR rig (commons/scenes/vr_staging.tscn with Godot XR Tools), the SKETCH helper (point, line, box), the joint pivots of ch12 as a helper, a two-colour palette Resource, the runnable kits in doc/book/studies/ (day-zero, point-zero, point-coordinates, point-lines, point-trace, random-definition), and an export preset. Skipped and covered by those parts: ch10 (pattern) and Parts III-VI; the camera, input and physics a visitor needs arrive inside the supplied walker and pickables.
tracks.mini_project: A family in drag (after Code as Creative Medium's 'Extrapolated Body' and 'Virtual Creature'): one body class of your own with one axis of four values, a written prediction of the closest pair, the comparison image and a one-sentence claim; the four members placed with one scanned or sculpted body in the small walkable room of your ch13 build; one debt comment in the code saying what the approximation owes. Shown to the class as a desktop build and, where a headset is available, walked in VR.

tracks.title: One year: the whole sketchbook and out of it
tracks.length: About 34 teaching weeks: six parts, each closed by a synthesis (ch07, ch13, ch16, ch21 midterm, ch27, ch39 capstone) followed by a pause week with no new code (Aesthetic Programming's rhythm); the final project is planned at ch36, two units before the end.
tracks.mini_project: Capstone: your own hall in Ada's endless museum, exported to the Quest, built from your families; the README holds a prediction, comparison image, claim and debt comment for each body (NoC's Ecosystem Project, turned into a museum room).

chapters.title: Day Zero: the instruction is the work
chapters.body: A LeWitt location drawing turned into one body: in the supplied base.tscn (floor, camera, light, Label3D) you type one line that calls a supplied place_at(where) and a cube appears at 'corner', 'midpoint' or 'centre'; one print() writes your instruction to the Output panel.

argument.predict: 'midpoint' and 'centre' will look most alike from the fixed camera (on a square floor both land on the middle line); 'somewhere near the middle' will not run at all.
argument.claim: An instruction a partner can interpret is not one the engine can run: ambiguity shows up as an error, not as a variation.

chapters.debt: LeWitt's drafters interpreted; the engine refuses. The planted bug (a misspelled node name) is the first debt: literalness is the price of repeatability. GDScript's English keywords are the default of programming (Marino on FLOW-MATIC), a cheap first question for Swedish-speaking students.
chapters.place: Itten's warm-up before the pencil: stand, reach and turn in the room (desktop, or the headset through the supplied walker); then a partner executes your written instruction on paper and you compare it with the run.
godot: project vs scene; F5 vs F6; save
an Inspector property edit seen in the running scene
reading an error in the Debugger
calling a supplied helper before writing any (use before make)

lineage.processing: LP ch2 Processing (run, errors); Handbook Structure 1 Code Elements
lineage.klee: Introduction: the teacher supplies phenomena; axiom 'to stand despite all possibilities to fall'
lineage.reference: Sol LeWitt, Paragraphs on Conceptual Art (1967) and Wall Drawing 159; Itten's Vorkurs warm-up; CCM 'Computing without a Computer'; Molnar's machine imaginaire

chapters.project_step: Start a sketchbook repository whose README will hold every prediction, comparison image, claim and debt comment of the course.

chapters.title: Point: a body with no size must be given one
chapters.body: A point built in _ready(): a MeshInstance3D whose SphereMesh radius is a variable, placed by setting its position property; then three points by hand, and a Label3D that counts the frames the engine has called you for.

argument.predict: 0.01 and 0.05 look most alike (both read as dots); 1.0 stops being a point and reads as a body or a plane.
argument.claim: A point is a relation between size and viewing distance: Kandinsky's point becomes a plane when it grows.

chapters.debt: Mathematically a point has no extent; to be seen it needs a mesh of hundreds of triangles. The engine can only show a point by lying about its size, the first approximation of the course.
chapters.place: Walk toward and away from the four points: the 0.25 m point changes category as you approach.

lineage.processing: LP ch1 Pixels (point, coordinates); Handbook Shape 1
lineage.klee: I.1 'the mobility agent is a point'
lineage.reference: Kandinsky, Point and Line to Plane: Point (size and shape); Fontana's buchi as the point that cuts (Ada BASE_LAYER.md)

chapters.project_step: Place three points whose sizes you chose; write your first PREDICTION.

chapters.title: Solid and ghost: one if decides what a body is
chapters.body: A row of bodies whose solid boolean decides, in one if, whether their collision shape is enabled and how opaque they are; the supplied make_solid() and make_ghost() are called before they are opened.

argument.predict: 'solid opaque' and 'ghost opaque' look identical except for the test ball dropped on each (resting on one, on the floor under the other).
argument.claim: What you see and what stops you are separate properties; collision is invisible until another body meets it.

chapters.debt: A still (and a screenshot) cannot show collision: the visual argument has a blind spot, and so do players. Invisible walls and walkable ghosts are the course's first uncanny.
chapters.place: Walk into each body: two stop you, two let you through, and one of the transparent ones surprises you.
godot: calling functions you did not write

lineage.klee: I.2-4 active, medial and passive lines (what acts and what is acted on)
lineage.reference: Kandinsky's polarities (repose against tension); GDQuest Learn GDScript lesson 3 (call supplied functions first)

chapters.project_step: Mark one of your points as a ghost and say in one sentence why.

chapters.title: Coordinates: carry the point
chapters.body: A carried point that writes its own Vector3 beside itself (Label3D), and a second point placed at an expression of the first (a + Vector3.UP, a * 0.5).

argument.axis: which axis the same length goes into
argument.predict: x and z look most alike from a standing eye; y does not, because up is the direction your body has.
argument.claim: The three axes are equal in the maths and unequal for a standing body: height is the one you feel.

chapters.debt: Godot's Y-up, metres and axis handedness are conventions baked into every later body; VR adds a default floor height that assumes a standing adult (Bagnall in Queer Game Studies on normativity in hardware).
chapters.place: Pick the point up (desktop carry, or an XR Tools pickable in the headset) and watch its coordinates change as you move it. Pickup belongs here, by the standing ruling.
godot: supplied XRToolsPickable and desktop carry; where the desktop rig is swapped for the XR rig

lineage.processing: LP ch1 coordinates; Handbook Shape 1 Coordinates
lineage.application_wp: pre-WP (the application names 'vectors' as a basic concept)
lineage.klee: II.14 three dimensions (borrowed early)
lineage.reference: LeWitt's corner, midpoint and centre as a coordinate system before Vector3

chapters.project_step: Put your three points in 3D, one of them above head height.

chapters.title: Line: distance belongs to the line
chapters.body: A segment between two carried points: your function show_between(a, b) places, scales and orients a thin box and returns the distance; a do-not-cross barrier reacts when that distance falls below a threshold (condition before threshold).

argument.axis: thickness as a fraction of length
argument.predict: 0.005 and 0.02 look most alike (both read as lines); 0.4 reads as a slab.
argument.claim: A line in 3D is a thin body: the ratio of thickness to length decides whether we read a line or a plane.

chapters.debt: The engine has no one-dimensional thing to show: the line is a box or an eight-sided cylinder pretending. Distance is a return value, and every later threshold is a design decision hidden as a number.
chapters.place: Hold both ends (two hands in the headset: Klee's maker 'who has only two hands') and stretch the line until it crosses the barrier.
godot: the supplied SKETCH helper line(a, b), opened

lineage.processing: LP ch7 Functions; Handbook Shape 1 line()
lineage.klee: I.1 an active line; I.3 a line limited by fixed points
lineage.reference: Kandinsky, Line (straight, angular, curved); the Point Lines kit

chapters.project_step: Connect two of your points with your own function, named after what it makes.

chapters.title: The walk: a line is a record
chapters.body: A trace recorder: the carried point appends its position to an array once it has moved further than a gate distance (list before append, condition before threshold), and a loop redraws the array as an ImmediateMesh line strip.

argument.predict: 0.01 and 0.05 look most alike (both read as continuous); 0.5 turns the walk into a polygon with visible corners.
argument.claim: A recorded line is a sampling decision: below a few centimetres the walk looks continuous, above it the corners become the drawing.

chapters.debt: Continuity is faked from a list. Memory is not free, so the trace must forget (a bounded array), and forgetting is a choice about which past counts.
chapters.place: Become the pen: the trace follows your hand (headset) or the carried point (desktop) while you walk a line through the hall, Klee's 'walk for a walk's sake'.

lineage.processing: LP ch6 Loops, ch9 Arrays (mouse history); Handbook Control 2 Repetition
lineage.noc: ch0 the random walk (as a later return)
lineage.klee: I.1 'an active line on a walk, moving freely, without goal'
lineage.reference: Klee I.1 (Point_Trace's final.md already cites it); Logo's turtle; Tilt Brush drawing in space (Queer 3D 2024)

chapters.project_step: Record one walk of your own and keep it as data in your project.

chapters.title: Plane: when the line closes
chapters.body: Close the walk: the recorded points become a triangle fan through SurfaceTool, normals are generated, and a collider made from the mesh lets you stand on the plane you walked.

argument.predict: 'clockwise flat' and 'reversed double-sided' look most alike from above; 'reversed' alone vanishes from the front.
argument.claim: A surface has a side: what you see of a plane is a promise its winding and normals make (Godot winds front faces clockwise).

chapters.debt: Culling (Gaboury, Image Objects ch1): hidden-surface algorithms decide what exists for the eye; a one-sided plane is invisible from behind while its collider still stops you. The fan also fails on concave walks: the approximation owes the shape its dents.
chapters.place: Stand on your walk: the plane made from your own trace becomes floor; walk to its edge and look under it.

lineage.processing: LP ch14 vertex shapes; Handbook Shape 2 Vertices
lineage.klee: I.2-4 'once completed, this linearity is replaced by planarity'
lineage.reference: Kandinsky, Basic Plane; Gaboury, Image Objects I 'Culling Vision'

chapters.project_step: SYNTHESIS I: your first room is one plane you walked, three points and one line. Commit it.

chapters.title: The chessboard: purely repetitive and therefore structural
chapters.body: A floor of cubes instanced from a PackedScene in a nested loop and coloured by a rule over (x, z) from a supplied palette of two materials.

argument.predict: The chessboard and the x%3 stripes look most alike from far away, where both read as texture; 'every cell' is the only floor without rhythm.
argument.claim: Structure is the repetition rule, not the cube: the same 64 bodies make four different floors.

chapters.debt: The grid is the unexamined ground of 3D (editor grids, voxels, Gaboury's frame buffer as a random-access grid). It is a choice, and the standing ruling holds that the first line did not need it.
chapters.place: Walk the floor; turn one cell into a ghost with Chapter 3's if and fall through it.

lineage.processing: LP ch6 nested loops; Handbook Control 2; Form+Code Repeat
lineage.klee: I.5-6 structural rhythm, the chessboard, 'purely repetitive and therefore structural'; I.7 divisional proportion 2:3:5
lineage.reference: Albers's constrained material: the two-colour palette is supplied like Color-aid paper

chapters.departure: array_tutorial (spine 3) comes before transformation (spine 2): Klee puts structure (I.5-8) before dimension (II), and Form+Code puts Repeat before Transform. Bodies can be repeated with position alone; the full transform waits for the organism (ch12).
chapters.project_step: Lay a floor for your room with a rhythm rule of your own.

chapters.title: Families: one body, one axis, a series
chapters.body: Describe a body in a single class: a class_name with two typed @export axes (for example rings and taper of a column), built procedurally in _ready(); a sweep instances four members side by side as a sheet.

argument.predict: 16 and 64 look most alike at 2 m; 4 is not a coarse sphere but another body, close to an octahedron.
argument.claim: Above about 16 segments a sphere stops paying visibly; below 8 it changes category: polycount decides which body you have.

chapters.debt: Polycount against smooth deformation (the application's topology question) and the triangle budget. A typed set() on a mistyped @export is refused in silence, so a sweep can publish four identical members and look finished (the project's own science_screen case).
chapters.place: Walk the sheet as a gallery wall; carry one member into your room.

lineage.processing: LP ch8 Objects (Zoog as a class); Handbook Shape 3 Parameters
lineage.klee: I.7 individual articulation by proportions; I.8 linear variation
lineage.reference: Vera Molnar's series and the 1%; Albers's controlled problem; CCSWG 2024 'describe it in a single class'; Generative Design's numbered variants

chapters.departure: A deliberate return to a late primitives hall (Primitives_Ignorance, spine 1): the family needs loops and instancing (ch8) first, and it must come before chance so that the seed can become an axis.
chapters.project_step: Turn one of your bodies into a class with two axes; write the closest-pair prediction before rendering its sheet.

chapters.title: Pattern: structure moves into the surface
chapters.body: A tile written pixel by pixel into an Image from a small 4x4 source kept as a Dictionary recipe, wrapped as an ImageTexture and repeated over your floor by UV scale; one get_color(x, y) method per symmetry rule.

argument.predict: pm and pg look most alike (both keep one mirror direction; the glide only shifts alternate rows).
argument.claim: The same sixteen pixels make four patterns: symmetry is a rule applied to a source, and the rule is what we see.

chapters.debt: Texture filtering and mipmaps blur the rule at a distance (nearest vs linear); the seventeen wallpaper groups are a closed classification that the ornament traditions they describe never needed.
chapters.place: Floor and walls of your room share one texture; walk away until the pattern reads as tone rather than tiles.

lineage.processing: Handbook Image 1; LP ch15 Images and Pixels
lineage.klee: I.6 quantitative structure moving into two dimensions (the chessboard)
lineage.reference: Recreating the Past: Pattern (Bridget Riley, Anni Albers); The Book of Shaders 'Patterns' as a later return (ch27)

chapters.departure: tiling (spine 5) before color (spine 4): colour is taught late, where Klee ends his book (ch26); until then the two-colour palette stays supplied.
chapters.project_step: Give your room one pattern of your own made from a 4x4 source.

chapters.title: Disturbed order: chance enters the grid
chapters.body: Schotter as a floor: your chessboard of cubes rotated and displaced by a seeded RandomNumberGenerator, more with every row; and 10 PRINT as a walkable maze (one of two rotations per cell).

argument.axis: disorder amplitude (maximum rotation in the last row)
argument.predict: 0 and 5 look most alike: the grid still reads. Somewhere between 5 and 20 it stops reading as a grid.
argument.claim: Randomness is visible only against a structure already built: the grid is what lets us see disorder.

chapters.debt: Computer randomness is pseudo-random: the same seed returns the same 'chance' (Random_Definition: a pattern that returns). Nake's question from Hommage a Paul Klee (1965): can a pseudo-random number stand in for intuition?
chapters.place: Walk down the Schotter floor until the disorder makes it unwalkable (the colliders follow the cubes); get lost in the 10 PRINT maze (10 PRINT's Maze Walker).

lineage.processing: LP ch4 random(); Handbook Math 4 Random
lineage.klee: absent from Klee: the lineage's first departure
lineage.reference: Frieder Nake, Hommage a Paul Klee 13/9/65 Nr. 2; Georg Nees, Schotter (1968); Vera Molnar, (Des)Ordres; 10 PRINT 'Regularity before Randomness'

chapters.departure: randomness (spine 10) is met a third of the way in: it enters Klee's lineage in 1965-68 as the disturbance of a grid already built (Nake, Nees, Molnar); the 2023 application puts it in WP1, Queer 3D's foundation asks 'what is randomness' first, and Code as Creative Medium places Unpredictability right after iteration. It returns as a game (ch21) and as noise (ch25, ch28).
chapters.project_step: Add a seeded disorder axis to your family and record the seed you keep.

chapters.title: The organism: bone, tendon, muscle
chapters.body: A limb of three segments as a parent-child chain with pivots, each joint turning by angle += speed * delta in _process (the course's first moving body); and Trans_Body's lattice that loses cells where a body passes.

argument.axis: where the pivot sits on each segment
argument.predict: 'at the end' and 'at one third' look most alike after 30 degrees; 'outside' makes the chain orbit instead of bend.
argument.claim: A body's motion is decided by where its joints are, not by what its parts look like.

chapters.debt: Klee maps active, medial and passive onto brain, muscle and bone, and onto male and female organs (I.9-12, verified in the Praeger text). The scene tree encodes the same command chain: the parent moves the child, never the reverse. Klee in drag starts here: make the passive bone drive (inverse kinematics follows in ch16).
chapters.place: Become it: attach the chain to your hand (headset) or the carried point and walk it through Trans_Body's lattice, carving a passage with your own movement ('chip from chip').

lineage.klee: I.9-12 bone, ligament, tendon and muscle; active/medial/passive; 'stone upon stone' against 'chip from chip'
lineage.reference: Gaboury, Image Objects IV 'Object Paradigms'; Processing Handbook's static-before-continuous order

chapters.departure: transformation (spine 2) comes after arrays, tiling and chance: Klee's organism follows structure (I.9 after I.5-8) and Form+Code puts Transform after Repeat; the still bodies of Part I needed only position. It also opens _process(delta) only now, as the Processing Handbook opens 'continuous' in its second part.
chapters.project_step: Give one body in your room a jointed part that moves.

chapters.title: Collage: a found body meets a made one
chapters.body: Recreate a precedent: the truncated solid of Durer's Melencolia I built procedurally, beside a body you scanned or drew in Tilt Brush or Blender and imported as glTF; one of the two is written with an AI assistant under the LeWitt protocol (you write the instruction, it writes the code, you check the wall).

argument.predict: The hand-coded and the AI-coded look most alike (same instruction, same primitives); the scan is the outlier by triangle count, not by silhouette.
argument.claim: How a body was made shows less in its silhouette than in its triangle count and its errors.

chapters.debt: Recreation (SFPC Recreating the Past): the difference between Durer's solid and yours is where the debt is written; the Melencolia hall already says its hidden surfaces 'are decisions we have made'. The AI's code guessed wherever your instruction was ambiguous. The scan has millions of triangles, holes and no inside; whose bodies get scanned?
chapters.place: A hybrid room (Queer 3D's ontology layer): imported and procedural bodies share one floor. Export a desktop build and show it, sharing early as Anthropy's Twine book does in its first chapter.
godot: Export dialog, templates, a desktop build
directing and checking generated GDScript: what should change, what must not, what observation would show it is wrong

lineage.application_wp: the application's commons (open, repair, change: Illich, Freire)
lineage.klee: I.12 additive and subtractive making, 'both time bound'
lineage.reference: Hannah Hoch and Bellmer (collage, Queer 3D 2024); the ReCode Project; LeWitt protocol for ai_assist; Durer, Melencolia I

chapters.departure: A deliberate return to the last primitives hall (Melencolia, spine 1) as Part II's synthesis; it closes the teaching half of the short track, which pivots into the mini project here.
chapters.project_step: SYNTHESIS II and the short track's pivot: export your room as a build with one found and one made body. The mini project starts from this build.

chapters.title: Eye level: the vertical axis moves with you
chapters.body: Railroad tracks: rails and ties made in a loop running to the horizon, seen by your own Camera3D whose height and field of view you change with input actions; a 'space box' is inserted at several depths.

argument.predict: 1.1 and 1.7 look most alike (horizon mid-frame, ties converging alike); 8 m flips the tracks into a plan.
argument.claim: Perspective is a fact about the eye's height, not about the tracks: the same geometry gives a plan or a corridor.

chapters.debt: The camera decides what exists (frustum, near plane; 'an iso view is half blind'), and VR's default height and IPD assume a standing adult body. Klee draws 'a house wall logically right but psychologically wrong'.
chapters.place: In the headset your head is the camera: crouch and the horizon moves with you. Trans_Scale scales the room by four and relocates you, so you are the scale that changed.
godot: scaling a room vs moving the eye

lineage.processing: LP ch14 Transformations and 3D; Handbook Transform 2
lineage.klee: II.14-20 railroad ties and perspective, the vertical axis that shifts with the viewer, eye level, space boxes
lineage.reference: Gaboury, Image Objects I (visibility); Queer Game Studies III (normativity in hardware)

chapters.departure: A second transformation hall after chance and the organism: Klee's dimension (II) follows structure and the organism (I).
chapters.project_step: Choose the eye height your room is made for, and write why.

chapters.title: The tightrope walker: balance
chapters.body: A stack of RigidBody3D blocks built in a loop with an offset per block (a tower whose pivots zig-zag around the vertical, Klee II.25), a mobile hung with joints (its recursive builder supplied), and a signal when the stack settles or falls.

argument.axis: centre-of-mass offset per block (fraction of block width)
argument.predict: 0 and 0.1 look most alike after settling (both stand); 0.3 leans and stands; 0.5 falls.
argument.claim: A body stands while its centre of mass is over its base: Klee's non-symmetrical balance is an equivalence of unequal parts, not a symmetry.

chapters.debt: Stability is a setting: solver iterations, sleep thresholds and the physics tick change the verdict (in this project a die read 15 of 16 at 90 Hz and 2 of 16 at 60 Hz). The engine's gravity is a global default nobody chose.
chapters.place: Stack the blocks with your own hands (XR pickables) until the tower holds; walk under the mobile.

lineage.klee: II.21-25 the tightrope walker 'is the scale'; non-symmetrical balance; disturbed and restored balance
lineage.reference: Moholy-Nagy's Vorkurs balance studies (c. 1924)

chapters.departure: formfinding (spine 8) before forces (spine 7): Klee's balance (II) precedes the gravitational curve (III). Stand the body before you push it: here the engine's gravity does the work; in Part IV you write gravity yourself.
chapters.project_step: Make one body in your room that must balance, and predict whether it holds.

chapters.title: Legs: the passive part drives
chapters.body: A plate on procedural legs: each foot finds the ground with a raycast and each leg chain is solved from the foot back to the hip (FABRIK), reversing Chapter 12's parent-child command.

argument.axis: number of legs under the same off-centre plate
argument.predict: 4 and 6 look most alike (both hold: their convex hull contains the centre of mass); 2 tips; 3 depends on where the centre sits.
argument.claim: Whether a body stands is decided by the convex hull of its feet, so the number of legs is an argument, not a style.

chapters.debt: Inverse kinematics lets the passive end (the foot, Klee's bone) drive the chain: the scene tree's hierarchy of command is a convention you can invert. IK also approximates (iterations, joint limits), and a leg finds only what its ray hits.
chapters.place: Walk your legged body across Trans_Pit's moving blocks; its feet re-plant as the ground moves.

lineage.klee: II.25 stumbling; I.9 bone as the passive organ, reversed
lineage.reference: Klee in drag (active and passive re-assigned); Critical Engineering Manifesto 6 (the machine includes bodies)

chapters.departure: A forces hall (spine 7) visited before the rest of forces: tip-or-hold belongs with balance, which is Klee's order.
chapters.project_step: SYNTHESIS III: a body in your room that finds its own footing.

chapters.title: The bullet: a curve made of steps
chapters.body: A thrown body whose path you integrate yourself (velocity += gravity * dt; position += velocity * dt), drawn as a predicted arc of 64 samples beside a plot of height against time; Change_Intro's Riemann sum is the same loop.

argument.predict: 1/60 and 1/240 look most alike; 1/10 lands visibly off the true parabola.
argument.claim: A computed trajectory is a sum of steps: the curve is the limit the steps approach, and a coarse step draws a different throw.

chapters.debt: Euler integration owes the curve its accuracy, and the frame rate becomes physics (delta vs a fixed step). The smooth curve you see is a polygon of decisions.
chapters.place: Throw it yourself (XR release velocity or a desktop launch) and stand where your prediction says it lands.

lineage.klee: III.26-30 'a bullet, fired at a steep angle, rises ... and falls to earth with accelerated energy'
lineage.reference: Change_Intro's secant and Riemann sum; Lague's naive-attempt-first form

chapters.departure: change (spine 6) after formfinding: the curve follows balance, as Klee's gravitational curve (III) follows balance (II).
chapters.project_step: Something in your room is thrown or falls along a curve you computed.

chapters.title: Regions with different laws
chapters.body: A balloon rising through stacked air strata: Area3D regions that each replace gravity and add drag (-b * velocity) for any body inside, applied with apply_central_force.

argument.predict: Vacuum and air look most alike over a short throw; water and honey both end in near-vertical falls.
argument.claim: A trajectory is a portrait of its medium, not of its thrower.

chapters.debt: Who writes the law? ProjectSettings holds one gravity for the world and an Area3D overrides it locally; linear drag is a guess at what real fluids do.
chapters.place: Walk into a region yourself: the player's gravity changes inside it (Klee's swimmer between water and air).

chapters.title: The meteor: an orbit that leaks
chapters.body: A small n-body system (a planet and a meteor deflected by it) stepped over an array of bodies; a headless test asserts that energy stays within a tolerance, and the debugger steps the integrator when it does not.

values: velocity Verlet at half the step
argument.predict: The two Verlet runs look most alike (closed orbits); explicit Euler spirals outward.
argument.claim: An orbit drawn by a computer is a property of its integrator: Euler invents energy, Verlet keeps it.

chapters.debt: The approximation owes energy: a planet that escapes is a numerical artefact, not physics. A test is an argument you can lose, and a green test on the wrong quantity is a recurring trap in this very project.

chapters.title: To stand despite all possibilities to fall: a round
chapters.body: A small complete game on Klee's axiom: stones that stand or sink after seeded random waits, a player who must stay upright, menu / play / fall / score as an enum state machine, a HUD, and the best time saved to user://.

argument.claim: Fairness in a chance game is visible: the telegraph turns randomness into something a body can answer.

chapters.debt: Seeded chance can be replayed and therefore learned: is the game random or a memory test? The score reduces a body's play to one number (Queer Game Studies IV on failure).

argument.claim: Period grows with the square root of length: the trace shows a law you cannot see in the swing.

chapters.debt: The small-angle formula is an approximation, and the numerical pendulum drifts (energy again). Klee's spinning top may fall in the engine anyway, since solver gyroscopics are approximate [mem: test it].

chapters.title: Circle and spiral: the question of life and death
chapters.body: The pendulum freed from gravity: a runner at (cos t, sin t); then the radius changes every turn, 2000 points along the spiral are drawn as one MultiMesh, and a walkable spiral ramp is built from the same function.

argument.predict: 0 and -20% look most alike in the first turn, but -20% dies in the centre; +20% and golden look alike until the third turn.
argument.claim: The sign of one number decides between the circle, the spiral that dies in the centre and the spiral that frees itself.

chapters.debt: Motion 'no longer finite' must be cut off, so the spiral needs a stop condition. The golden spiral carries a myth of nature's law: Fibonacci as norm is a claim to test, not to teach. One MultiMesh instead of 2000 nodes: the frame budget is also a debt.

chapters.title: Sound: the swing heard

argument.predict: Sine and triangle look (and sound) most alike; square and noise are outliers in different ways.
argument.claim: The shape you see is the timbre you hear: corners are overtones.

chapters.debt: Sampling rate and bit depth make the wave discrete; the square's corners alias; additive synthesis (Synthesis_Lab) is Fourier's claim that every shape is a sum of circles.

chapters.title: A colour has many faces
chapters.body: A strip of bodies coloured between two complementary colours by lerp in RGB and in HSV, from a palette saved as your own Resource (.tres) and shared by their materials; one albedo placed under two lamps.

argument.predict: RGB lerp and the stepped bands look most alike at a distance; RGB lerp passes through Klee's central grey, HSV through the colour circle.
argument.claim: The grey in the middle belongs to the RGB space, not to the colours: the same two ends give a grey or a rainbow.

chapters.debt: A colour is never one value: sRGB against linear, tone mapping, the lamp, the headset's display. Albers's universal eye and Klee's colour spiritualism are claims. A shared Resource makes every body change colour at once: the bug is the lesson in sharing.

chapters.title: Rules in time: cellular automata

chapters.debt: Determinism can look like chance (rule 30 has served as a random generator [mem]); 'complexity from simple rules' hides who chose the rule and the edges (wrap or wall).

chapters.title: The tree and its mad branch: recursion
chapters.body: Munari's tree as a recursive function: the trunk splits in two, each branch thinner by a ratio, until a base case; a seeded 'mad branch' breaks the rule once.

argument.predict: 0.7 and 0.8 look most alike in silhouette (both dense crowns); 0.5 reads as a bare fork.
argument.claim: The ratio, not the depth, decides whether a tree reads as a tree; the mad branch shows that the family survives its exception.

chapters.debt: 'Recursion must always be controlled' (Queer 3D): without a base case the stack overflows (the planted bug) and the frame freezes; an explicit-stack version with a per-frame budget is the repair. Botanical naturalness as a norm; the mad branch as a queer reading.

learned_from: Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook (verified text): its four parts give the macro-order; its correction to the project's own summary matters (pendulum and top open Part IV, not gravity; circle and spiral are derived from the pendulum; the book ends in colour), so colour is taught late and the pendulum-circle-spiral chain is one derivation (ch22-23).

Klee's Part I is a body book (bone, tendon, muscle; heart and blood; 'the tightrope walker is the scale'); its active/medial/passive trichotomy mapped onto male and female is the precise place for 'in drag': the scene tree's parent-child command chain is taught (ch12) and then inverted by IK (ch16).

Kandinsky, Point and Line to Plane: Part I's three steps and its polarity questions (when does a point become a plane; when does a line become a slab) become the first ARGUMENT axes (ch02, ch05); the basic plane is a subject, not a given (ch07-08).

Albers, Interaction of Color: every ARGUMENT is a controlled problem with a stated visual target in one constrained material, variants compared side by side, theory after experience; the supplied two-colour palette is his coloured paper, and 'make one colour look like two' is ch26's place.

Nake (Hommage a Paul Klee, 1965), Nees (Schotter), Molnar ((Des)Ordres, the series and the 1%): randomness enters the Klee lineage as disturbance of a grid already built, which fixes its place right after the chessboard and families (ch11), a declared departure from spine 10 matching the application's WP1.
Processing Handbook (2007): static before continuous (delta waits until ch12), a synthesis closing each part, and debugging as a chapter of its own mid-course (ch20).

Learning Processing / GDQuest Learn GDScript: call supplied functions before defining them, the planted error early, one student body rebuilt as each idea arrives (the student's room and family are carried through every project_step).

Aesthetic Programming: pause weeks without new syntax after each synthesis, peer feedback on each week's work, the ReadMe beside the code in Git (the sketchbook README), and the final project planned two units before the end (ch36).

Critical Code Studies and the CCSWG: 'describe it in a single class' (ch09), the confessing comment turned into a student's debt comment (ch13 onward), and a code-critique station on Ada's own supplied code at the DEBT step, never at the opening (ch34, after Marino on Kittler's raytracer); Chun's 'sourcery' as the dark spot of 'revealing the black box'.
